source.title: Composed Fine-Tuning: Freezing Pre-Trained Denoising Autoencoders for Improved Generalization
source.authors: Sang Michael Xie; Tengyu Ma; Percy Liang

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports in-distribution generalization results for composed fine-tuning on structured-output tasks, but it does not test any of the listed versions about random-label memorization, width, image CNNs versus fully connected networks, optimizers, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized-example removal.
record.gate_note: The theory compares minimum-norm predictors with and without a denoiser, and experiments report test accuracy and compilation on structured-output tasks. These results do not measure the training–test gap or a listed version. OOD results are outside the claim’s scope.
record.test_reason: The study compares fine-tuning methods for structured-output prediction and proves representational norm bounds. None tests V1–V8. Its dropout result concerns font-image generation MSE, whereas V6 concerns classifier error; using dropout elsewhere without an ablation also does not test V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors argue that standard fine-tuning fails to fully exploit pre-trained output structure and that frozen-denoiser composition simplifies the base predictor and improves tested in-distribution and OOD performance. The simplification is established theoretically for a restricted function family; the empirical gains are conditional, with a larger standard fine-tuned model outperforming the smaller composed model on SansType OOD accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a predictor composed with a frozen denoiser for structured-output prediction; it does not use the original claim’s random-label memorization setup or measure a training–test gap.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported gains vary by dataset and split; on S ANS T YPE, the larger-denoiser standard fine-tuning model exceeds composed fine-tuning on the OOD split. OOD results are outside the claim’s scope.

fits_no_version.finding: Composed fine-tuning raises in-distribution correct-output accuracy from 79.8% to 84.4% on SansType and from 37.0% to 38.1% on SPoC TestW.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Composing a predictor with a frozen pre-trained denoiser can improve held-out correctness on structured-output translation tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Successful compilation rises from 86.8% to 90.4% on SansType and from 52.5% to 53.9% on SPoC TestW.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Composed fine-tuning can improve generated-code compilation rates over standard fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6.3 reports that adding dropout to the composed font-image generator reduces test MSE from 0.171 to 0.165.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout can improve pixelwise prediction error for a composed font-image generator on unseen font-character combinations.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5 proves that composing with an ideal projection denoiser can substantially reduce the minimum representational norm for a specified family of piecewise-constant targets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output-validity projections can reduce the representational complexity required of a base predictor.

record.problems: The experiments do not report training error, so they cannot establish changes to the training–test gap. The results concern structured-output prediction with a pre-trained denoiser, not the natural-label and random-label setting in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: OOD results in Table 2 and Tables 3–5, ablations and alternative fine-tuning comparisons in Tables 1, 3, 4, and 5, and image-generation test MSE are not extracted because they do not measure a listed version; OOD results are explicitly outside scope. The theoretical norm bounds in Section 5 compare representational complexity rather than measured generalization gaps.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe, including chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error. Layer-count comparisons and unbounded-width representation theory do not test this.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, including the role of local connectivity and initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects on classifier held-out error, small-training-set exceptions, excessive-dropout underfitting, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, its correlation with generalization gaps, and ranking against other measures. Representational norm bounds do not measure sharpness.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation='tests' is inconsistent with its correctly assigned T6. The decisive issue is mismatch with the specified versions, rather than the absence of training-error measurements: most versions can be tested with appropriate held-out comparisons alone. All extracted rows are method-performance comparisons outside V1–V8. The font-generation dropout result also falls outside V6 because it measures generation MSE rather than classifier error. No omitted result warrants a listed-version verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization on the same architectures and training recipes.
A width sweep beyond the zero-training-error threshold and its effect on test error.
A comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks on image classification.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD on held-out performance.
Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout effects on held-out error in the listed classifier regimes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training–test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
